headline: Local Codes and Seismic Standards for Foundation Repair
articleBody: ### Impact of Local Codes and Seismic Standards on Foundation Repair Foundation repair contractors in Los Angeles County must follow the **California Building Code (CBC)** as adopted and amended by local jurisdictions, along with specific **seismic design requirements** for a high-risk earthquake region. The CBC classifies much of Los Angeles as a high seismic design category, which affects allowable details for anchorage, reinforcement, and lateral resistance in foundations when repairs rise to the level of structural alteration. Local building departments, including the Los Angeles County Department of Public Works and city building and safety divisions, require permits for most structural foundation repairs. Their guidance explains that work such as underpinning, new grade beams, adding hold-downs, or installing new foundation segments typically needs **engineered plans** and inspections at key stages. In practice, this means repair methods often must be designed or approved by a **licensed structural engineer**, particularly on hillsides or in soft/expansive soil zones. Seismic retrofit programs and ordinances in various Los Angeles-area cities outline prescriptive measures for older homes, such as installing **anchor bolts, cripple wall bracing, and plywood shear panels** between foundation and superstructure. These same standards influence how contractors tie new or repaired foundation elements into existing structures to improve earthquake performance. Technical manuals from California earthquake safety initiatives note that repairs should not reduce seismic capacity and, when feasible, should improve it. Additionally, geotechnical reports may be required in landslide or liquefaction zones identified by state seismic hazard maps. In these areas, acceptable repair methods can include **deepened footings, drilled piers/caissons, or grade beams** tailored to site conditions. Consequently, Los Angeles foundation repairs are shaped heavily by seismic safety priorities, requiring code-compliant, engineered solutions rather than purely cosmetic or informal fixes.
